Water leaking onto a floor forms a circular pool. The radius of the pool increases at a rate of $6\,\text{cm/min}.$ How fast is the area of the pool increasing at the moment when the radius is $\frac{2}{\pi }\,\text{cm}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=\frac{2}{\pi },$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=6.$

To start, let's write down the area formula for the circle and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=6$ and $r=\frac{2}{\pi },$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =6\cdot 2\pi (\frac{2}{\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the area of the pool is increasing at a rate of $24{\text{ cm}}^{2}\text{/min}.$

A snowball is melting in the sun and slowly shrinking. Determine the rate at which the surface area of the snowball is decreasing, given that the radius is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{1}{5}\,\text{in/s}$ and its surface area at that moment is $100\pi \,{\text{in}}^{2}.$ Do not round the answer.

*Hint*: Assume that the rate of decrease is positive.

The surface area of the snowball is decreasing at a rate of 
{{field-1}} ${\text{in}}^{2}/\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the snowball and let $A$ be its surface area. Both $r$ and $A$ change with time. In particular, we are given that

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{5}\,\text{in/s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ when $A=100\pi \,{\text{in}}^{2}.$

To start, let's write down the formula for the surface area of a sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 8\pi r\end{aligned}
$$

We then calculate the value of $r$ using $A=100\pi .$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ 100\pi  & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ 25 & ={r}^{2} \\ r & =\pm 5\end{aligned}
$$

Since radius cannot be negative, we have $r=5.$

We now substitute $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{5}$ and $r=5$ into our expression for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{5}\cdot 8\pi \cdot 5 \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the surface area of the snowball is decreasing at a rate of $8\pi \,{\text{in}}^{2}\text{/s}.$

A small, circular puddle evaporates on a floor. If the puddle’s area is decreasing at a rate of $32\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{2}/\text{min},$ calculate the rate of change of its circumference at the moment when the radius is $8\,\text{cm}.$ Do not round the answer.

The circumference of the puddle is decreasing at a rate of 
{{field-1}} $\text{cm}/\text{min}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=8,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-32\pi .$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

When $r=8\,\text{cm},$ $C=2\pi (8)=16\pi \text{ cm}.$ Hence, substituting $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-32\pi $ and $C=16\pi ,$ and solving for $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-32\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{16\pi }{2\pi } \\ -32\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot 8 \\ \frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =-4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the circumference is decreasing at a rate of $4\pi \text{ cm}\text{/min}.$

A spherical hailstone is melting uniformly, causing its radius to change at a rate of $\frac{1}{6\pi }\,\text{mm}\text{/s}.$ If the radius at a certain moment is $15\,\text{mm},$ what is the rate at which the surface area is decreasing?

The surface area of the hailstone is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} ${\text{mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the hailstone and $A$ its surface area. Both $r$ and $A$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{6\pi }\,\text{mm}\text{/s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=15\,\text{mm}.$

To start, let's write down the surface area formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}8\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{6\pi }$ and $r=15.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{6\pi }\cdot 8\pi (15) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-20.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the surface area of the hailstone is decreasing at a rate of $20{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the hailstone, $V$ the volume, and $A$ its surface area. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the volume $V$ and the surface area $A$ of the sphere. Since $A=4\pi {r}^{2}$ and $V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3},$ the relationship between $V$ and $A$ is

$$
V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3}=\frac{4\pi }{3}{(\frac{A}{4\pi })}^{3/2}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{3(4\pi )^{1/2}}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}A}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }} \\ {A}^{1/2} & =12\sqrt{\pi } \\ A & =(12\sqrt{\pi })^{2} \\ A & =144\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $A=4\pi {r}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4\pi {r}^{2} & =144\pi  \\ {r}^{2} & =36 \\ r & =6.\end{aligned}
$$
